Unlike past fee hikes—which were incremental adjustments for fraud prevention or asylum processing—this episode resembles the aggressive tariff-style regulatory shocks seen in trade policy rather than traditional immigration rulemaking, representing a qualitative shift toward using absolute cost as a protectionist lever.

The structural friction of bureaucratic drag and judicial challenges rarely achieves a permanent bar at the final rule stage unless the underlying statutory delegation is completely absent, which is not the case for fee-setting authorities in immigration adjudication. The structural friction points—specifically mandatory OIRA interagency coordination, the Paperwork Reduction Act compliance mechanisms, and inevitable federal court preliminary injunctions triggered by predictable procedural flaws in justifying a nearly 1,000-fold fee hike—historically succeed in delaying or halting rules of this magnitude. Federal courts frequently intervene to block arbitrary and capricious agency actions where economic justifications are legally fragile, and the baseline historical failure rate of major contested immigration regulations reaching final enactment unmolested under stringent APA review is exceptionally high.
